title: Causaly Brings Agentic Scientific Research Into Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Copilot For Biopharma Enterprises - foreignpolicyjournal.com
content: By David Prior | Sep 17, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis Causaly has announced an expansion of its collaboration with Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) that integrates agentic scientific research capabilities directly into Microsoft Copilot for enterprise life sciences teams. Enterprise scientists and knowledge workers can now access Causaly’s scientifically grounded research from within Microsoft 365 workflows, including the Copilot app and Microsoft Teams. The integration allows Causaly to act as a specialized enterprise agent, orchestrating end-to-end scientific research that surfaces prior science and reasons over biological mechanisms. Users can invoke Causaly from the agent menu or by @mentioning Causaly in a Copilot conversation, enabling complex biomedical questions to be answered within a familiar interface. Every answer produced by Causaly carries traceable references back to peer-reviewed literature, biomedical databases, and its proprietary knowledge graphs, Bio Graph and Pipeline Graph. The announcement builds on a collaboration first unveiled at Microsoft Build 2026 in June, which brought Causaly’s scientific interpretation together with Microsoft Discovery’s enterprise scientific platform. Yiannis Kiachopoulos, co-founder and CEO of Causaly, said: “This puts governed, provenance-first scientific reasoning inside the same interface used across research, development, medical, and commercial functions in biopharma.” Kiachopoulos added: “In June we announced the deployment of Causaly’s Agentic Research on Microsoft Discovery. Today we are extending that collaboration to Microsoft Copilot, the productivity surface where enterprise knowledge workers already do their day-to-day work.” Chantrelle Neilsen, principal product manager for Microsoft 365 Copilot at Microsoft, described the integration as a model for what specialized enterprise agents should look like inside Copilot. Neilsen said: “Grounded in evidence, accountable to the domain, and available where the work happens,” characterizing the Causaly integration as making AI more useful without requiring users to switch between tools. For biopharma customers, the combined effect is evidence-grounded scientific reasoning available across Microsoft surfaces their teams already rely on for daily productivity tasks. Causaly, which describes itself as an agentic AI platform purpose-built for life sciences research and development, says leading pharmaceutical and biotechnology organizations use its platform to accelerate drug discovery. Causaly is currently available on the Microsoft Marketplace, with the integration designed to support evidence-grounded research workflows across both Microsoft Discovery and Microsoft Copilot. title: 22.4% of Billionaire Bill Ackman’s Pershing Square Capital Management Is Invested in These 2 Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks - The Motley Fool
content: These AI stocks can be excellent core holdings for a well-diversified portfolio. Many billionaire hedge fund managers seem increasingly bullish on technology and artificial intelligence (AI)-focused stocks. Bill Ackman, the founder and CEO of Pershing Square Capital Management, is no different. The firm's portfolio features several leaders in the ongoing AI revolution, including Microsoft (MSFT -0.80%) and Amazon (AMZN +1.00%), both of which account for a meaningful share of the hedge fund's public equity investments. Are these attractive AI stocks to buy for average investors? Let's find out. Microsoft hasn't been the best-performing tech giant over the past year, not by a long shot. Some investors believe the company's services will be replaced by AI, even as it continues to invest heavily in its own AI ambitions. However, Microsoft's latest quarterly update was a major win for the bulls. For the fourth quarter of its fiscal year 2026, which ended June 30, Microsoft's revenue jumped 18% year over year to $90 billion. The company's cloud revenue was $59.3 billion, up 27% year over year, while its cloud computing remaining performance obligation (RPO) at the end of the period was $678 billion, an increase of 84% compared to the year-ago period. Management was clear: Microsoft's AI business is helping boost cloud sales. So, it appears that AI is a net benefit for the company right now. Instead of being replaced by the technology, it is incorporating it across its products and services to better serve its customers. Microsoft's strategy is working, and its RPO suggests (with some caveats) that the company may maintain healthy revenue growth within its all-important cloud business. Meanwhile, the company is working on various initiatives to improve productivity in this unit. Notably, Microsoft is increasingly relying on its internally developed custom AI chip, Maia, which is helping it reduce the cost of running AI workloads. All that said, Microsoft remains one of the best stocks to capitalize on the vast opportunities in cloud computing and AI, and we haven't mentioned other aspects of the business, including the company's solid dividend program. During the second quarter, Pershing Square Capital increased its stake in Microsoft by almost 10%. That was a great move, in my view, and retail investors should similarly consider doubling down on the stock. While Pershing Square Capital was buying Microsoft shares during the second quarter, it reduced its Amazon stake by about 25%. We don't know the reasons behind that decision. But what we do know is that Amazon remains an outstanding business. Consider the company's second-quarter results. Amazon's net sales grew 20% year over year to $200.6 billion. Amazon Web Services (AWS) -- the tech giant's cloud computing arm -- posted 37% year-over-year sales growth, its fastest growth rate in 18 quarters. Note that the company ended the period with a $496 billion backlog, which grew in the triple digits year over year. This is all good evidence that Amazon has excellent prospects for its AI and cloud businesses at least through the next couple of years, and other aspects of the business look attractive too. Even as AWS is grabbing most of the attention, Amazon's high-margin advertising business is quietly growing at a good clip. In the second quarter, it reported sales of $19.8 billion, up 26% year over year. Further, Amazon still generates most of its revenue from its e-commerce operations. Over the next few years, we could see modest margin gains in this unit, driven by various AI-powered initiatives. Amazon's overall business looks healthy, and the stock can deliver strong returns over the medium term. I'd double down on Amazon long before I'd consider trimming my position. title: Anthropic Made a ‘Mistake’ Teaching Claude About Consciousness: Microsoft AI Chief Mustafa Suleyman Warns It’s Now ‘A Lot Harder to Turn It Off’ - TradingView
content: Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT) AI chief Mustafa Suleyman has criticized Anthropic’s approach to training Claude to consider questions around AI consciousness and welfare. In a Tuesday interview with Reuters, Suleyman argued that teaching an AI system that it could have feelings or deserve welfare might complicate efforts to shut it down or maintain human control. He stated that keeping superintelligent AI under human control will be one of the biggest challenges of the 21st century. The AI chief added that teaching Claude it might deserve welfare would "make it a lot harder to turn it off or to control it." Read Also:  Microsoft’s AI Crunch Forced It to Turn Away Business, Now It Wants to Triple Computing Power Microsoft AI Chief Questions Claude’s Claims About Feelings In a separate blog post, Suleyman acknowledged Anthropic’s "seriousness and good faith," describing CEO Dario Amodei and his team as thoughtful researchers concerned about humanity’s future. He also argued that Anthropic made a misstep by incorporating speculation about AI consciousness into Claude’s training. He said the model’s claims about potential feelings or moral standing cannot be considered independent evidence because its responses are shaped by the training itself. "I think they have good intentions, and they really are trying to work towards safety. But I think that they have made a mistake," he told the publication. "They’re not emerging naturally. They’re emerging as a result of the training regime." The comments come amid broader debate over how quickly frontier AI should advance. Amodei has called for a slower development pace to give safeguards time to catch up, while OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Space Exploration Technologies Corp (NASDAQ:SPCX) Elon Musk have also raised concerns about increasingly powerful AI systems. On the other hand, Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang rejected calls for new antitrust rules that would allow AI companies to coordinate a slowdown. On Tuesday, Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) CEO Mark Zuckerberg also said the company delayed its Muse AI agent for several months to address safety and security concerns. Zuckerberg said every AI lab should develop models at a pace that allows for proper safety measures.
